analogy: An LLM judge is a new referee. Before you let them run the final, you watch them call 50 recorded plays and compare their calls with a panel of experienced referees. If they agree far more often than chance, you trust them; if they always favour the team on the left side of the screen, you swap the sides and see if the call changes. The analogy breaks because a human referee can explain each call; an LLM judge's reasons can sound good and still be wrong, so you check agreement in numbers, not in explanations.

scale.title: Validating a faithfulness judge before it gates releases of a 500-question RAG suite
scale.html:
Assumptions: a 500-question RAG golden set, an LLM judge that labels each answer faithful or not, and 50 answers hand-labelled by two engineers.

  1. Agreement table on the 50. Both say faithful: 27. Human yes, judge no: 3. Human no, judge yes: 5. Both no: 15.
  2. Raw agreement. (27 + 15) / 50 = 0.84.
  3. Chance agreement. Humans say yes 30/50 = 0.60, the judge 32/50 = 0.64. p_e = 0.60 x 0.64 + 0.40 x 0.36 = 0.384 + 0.144 = 0.528.
  4. Cohen's kappa. (0.84 - 0.528) / (1 - 0.528) = 0.312 / 0.472 = 0.66. Usable, but look at the 5 cases where the judge passed answers humans failed: those are the dangerous ones for a faithfulness gate. Tighten the rubric ("any number not in the context is unsupported") and re-measure.
  5. Compare v1 and v2 on 500. Net score moved from 80.0% to 82.4%. But only the flipped questions carry signal: v2 fixed 31, broke 19. McNemar's test: (|31 - 19| - 1)2 / (31 + 19) = 121 / 50 = 2.42, below the 3.84 needed for p < 0.05. Not yet a proven win.
  6. RAG metrics follow the same rule. Faithfulness, answer relevance and context precision and recall in the Ragas style are all judge outputs (Es et al., arXiv 2309.15217), so each needs this calibration, and the judge model and prompt must stay fixed when you compare versions. Change the judge and you changed the ruler.

lab.look_for: The lab's position-bias test swaps the A/B order and counts how many verdicts flip; that flip rate is your judge's position bias in one number. The regression gate compares two prompt versions per case, so list the cases that flipped in each direction and run the McNemar arithmetic above on them. Also look at the LLM-as-judge faithfulness score: hand-label 20 of its verdicts yourself and compute kappa before you trust it.

quiz.q: Your judge agrees with humans on 90% of items, but 90% of all answers are good. Why is 90% agreement not impressive here?

options.t: A judge that says "good" to everything would also agree about 90% of the time; kappa corrects for this chance agreement.
options.why: With skewed classes, raw agreement is inflated. If both rate 90% as good independently, chance agreement is 0.9 x 0.9 + 0.1 x 0.1 = 0.82, so 90% observed gives kappa = (0.90 - 0.82) / 0.18 = 0.44, only moderate.

options.t: Because 90% is below the 95% industry standard.
options.why: There is no universal 95% bar. The issue is that raw agreement ignores how much agreement chance alone would produce.

options.t: Because humans are always right, so any disagreement is fatal.
options.why: Humans disagree with each other too; you often measure human-human kappa as the ceiling. The problem here is chance agreement, not human infallibility.

options.t: It is impressive; 90% agreement means the judge is reliable.
options.why: Not with a 90% base rate. The judge may be useless at catching the 10% of bad answers, which are the ones you built it to catch.

quiz.q: After switching the judge to a newer model, your RAG system's faithfulness score jumps from 0.78 to 0.86 with no change to the system. What is the right conclusion?

options.t: The ruler changed, not the system: re-calibrate the new judge against human labels and re-score the old baseline with it before comparing anything.
options.why: A judge-scored metric is the judge's opinion. A new judge may be more lenient. Scores are comparable only when produced by the same judge, prompt and rubric.

options.t: The system got better; newer judges are more accurate.
options.why: Nothing about the system changed. A newer judge may be more lenient or stricter, and neither is accuracy until you check it against humans.

options.t: Average the two scores to get the true value.
options.why: Averaging two uncalibrated rulers gives a third uncalibrated number.

options.t: Faithfulness cannot be measured by LLMs at all.
options.why: It can, as in the Ragas paper, once the judge is validated. The mistake is comparing scores across judges.

exercises.q: On 100 items: both pass 70, human pass and judge fail 5, human fail and judge pass 10, both fail 15. Compute raw agreement and Cohen's kappa.
exercises.a: Raw agreement = (70 + 15) / 100 = 0.85. Human pass rate = (70 + 5) / 100 = 0.75; judge pass rate = (70 + 10) / 100 = 0.80. Chance agreement = 0.75 x 0.80 + 0.25 x 0.20 = 0.60 + 0.05 = 0.65. Kappa = (0.85 - 0.65) / (1 - 0.65) = 0.20 / 0.35 = 0.57. Moderate. The 10 items the judge passed but humans failed are the risk; read them and fix the rubric.

exercises.q: Prompt v2 beats v1 on a 300-question set: 74% vs 70%. Per question, v2 fixed 22 and broke 10. Is this a real improvement at the 5% level?
exercises.a: Net gain = 22 - 10 = 12 questions = 4 points of 300. McNemar with continuity correction: (|22 - 10| - 1)^2 / (22 + 10) = 121 / 32 = 3.78. The 5% critical value for 1 degree of freedom is 3.84, so it is just short. Call it promising, not proven: add questions or repeat runs, and read the 10 regressions, since a fix that breaks a safety-critical case may not be worth 22 small wins.

exercises.q: You run Ragas-style faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision and context recall in CI on every pull request. Design the safeguards so the numbers deserve trust.
exercises.a:
• Calibrate each judged metric. Hand-label 50-100 items per metric, compute kappa (or correlation for scores), and keep the labels as a regression test for the judge itself.
  • Pin the ruler. Version the judge model, prompt and rubric. When any changes, re-score the baseline before comparing.
  • Know what each metric cannot see. Faithfulness ignores whether the context was right; answer relevance (Ragas uses generated-question similarity) does not check factual accuracy; context recall needs reference answers; context precision rises if you return less. So pair them, and add answer correctness on a referenced subset.
  • Quantify noise. Bootstrap confidence intervals or paired tests on the same questions; gate on "significantly worse", not "any drop".
  • Avoid self-preference. Use a judge from a different model family from the generator where possible.
  • Watch for gaming. Track abstention rate and answer length so a system cannot raise faithfulness by saying less.

interview.q: What is position bias in an LLM judge and how do you handle it?
interview.a: Position bias is when a judge comparing two answers tends to prefer whichever it sees first (or second), regardless of quality. You handle it by judging each pair twice with the order swapped and only counting a win when both orders agree; disagreement becomes a tie. You can also measure it directly: the fraction of pairs whose verdict flips when swapped is the judge's position-bias rate, and it should be low before you trust the judge.

interview.q: How do you validate an LLM-as-judge for RAG faithfulness before using it?
interview.a: I sample 50 to 100 real answers with their retrieved context and have two people label each claim or answer as supported or not, using the same rubric the judge gets. I check human-human agreement first, which is my ceiling. Then I run the judge and compute Cohen's kappa against the consensus, and I read the confusion matrix, because for a gate the key number is how often the judge passes answers humans failed. If kappa is weak I fix the rubric, add examples, or try a stronger judge, and re-measure. I keep the labelled set to re-check whenever the judge changes.

interview.q: A dashboard shows faithfulness 0.91 and answer relevancy 0.88 from Ragas, and leadership wants to ship. What might these numbers hide?
interview.a: Several things. Both are reference-free, so neither says whether answers are correct: faithfulness only checks support by the retrieved context, which may be stale, and Ragas's answer relevancy scores how well questions generated from the answer match the user question, and its docs say it does not evaluate factual accuracy. Neither measures retrieval coverage; context recall needs references. A system that abstains or says little can score high faithfulness. Judges have position, verbosity and self-preference bias, so I need kappa against human labels and a judge from a different family from the generator. And I want confidence intervals, slices by query type, and a check that the golden set matches production traffic. Then decide.

analogy: Text-to-SQL is a translator between a manager and a filing clerk. The manager says "how much did Canada spend?"; the translator turns it into the clerk's exact instructions: which drawer, which folders, how to add up. A good translator knows the filing system cold. The analogy breaks because a human translator who is unsure asks "which Canada figure, gross or net?"; a model will usually just pick one and hand back a confident number.

scale.title: Is text-to-SQL worth it for a 1,500-person company's analyst queue?
scale.html:
Assumptions: 1,500 employees, 300 ad-hoc data questions a week, 20 analyst minutes each, a model at $2 / $10 per million input / output tokens (claude-sonnet-5-5, Anthropic models overview, checked 2026-11-03), 4,000 tokens of schema context and 200 output tokens per call, 1.3 calls per question on average (retries).

  1. Today's cost in people. 300 x 20 min = 6,000 min = 100 hours a week, about 2.5 full-time analysts doing nothing but queue work.
  2. Model cost. One call = 4,000 x $2 / 1 M + 200 x $10 / 1 M = $0.008 + $0.002 = $0.01. With 1.3 calls, $0.013 a question, about $3.90 a week. Cost is not the decision.
  3. Correctness is. Suppose your golden set shows 85% execution accuracy. That leaves 15% x 300 = 45 wrong answers a week. Some fail loudly (errors, empty results); the rest are wrong-but-runs, confident numbers in someone's slide deck.
  4. Design for the 45. Show the SQL and row count with every answer, send ambiguous questions back with a clarifying question, restrict the model to curated views, and route anything feeding finance or board reporting to an analyst for review.
  5. Realistic payoff. If 70% of questions are simple lookups the system handles well and analysts review the rest, the queue drops by about 70 hours a week, and analysts spend their time on the hard 30% and on the semantic layer that makes the easy 70% safe.

lab.look_for: The lab runs text-to-SQL on DuckDB with schema grounding, a SELECT-only validator, a row limit, a self-correction loop and execution-accuracy scoring over a small question set. For this lesson, look at the failures in the scoring output and sort them into this page's buckets: ambiguity, schema misunderstanding, wrong-but-runs, dialect. Pay most attention to any question where the SQL ran but the result did not match the expected answer: that is the dangerous class.

quiz.q: The model answers "total revenue per customer" with SUM(o.amount) after joining orders to order_items (several items per order). What goes wrong?

options.t: Each order's amount is repeated once per item row, so revenue is inflated; the query runs fine and returns a confident wrong number.
options.why: This is join fan-out. An order of $120 with 3 items becomes 3 rows of $120 and sums to $360. No error is raised, which makes it the wrong-but-runs failure.

options.t: The database raises an error because amount is ambiguous.
options.why: With the o. prefix the column is not ambiguous. The query is valid SQL; its logic is wrong.

options.t: Nothing; joins never change sums.
options.why: Joins to a finer-grained table multiply rows. Aggregating a coarse-grained column after that join double counts.

options.t: Only the row order changes.
options.why: The totals change, not just the order. That is why understanding table grain matters.

exercises.q: Which of these questions are ambiguous, and what clarifying question would you ask? (a) "Orders last month" (b) "Our best customers" (c) "Revenue in Canada in 2025"
exercises.a: (a) Slightly: calendar month or last 30 days, and count or value? Ask "Do you mean the number of orders in October 2026?" (b) Very: best by revenue, order count, margin or recency? Ask "Best by total paid revenue, by number of orders, or something else?" (c) Mostly clear, but gross or net of refunds and by billing or shipping country. A semantic layer that defines revenue once removes most of the doubt.

exercises.q: orders(id, customer_id, amount) has order 55 with amount 120.00, and order_items(order_id, product_id, qty) has 3 rows for order 55. Write the wrong query a model might produce for "revenue from order 55", give its result, and write the correct one.
exercises.a: Wrong: SELECT SUM(o.amount) FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id WHERE o.id = 55; returns 360.00, because the join produces 3 rows each carrying 120.00. Correct: SELECT amount FROM orders WHERE id = 55; returning 120.00. If you need item data too, aggregate items in a subquery first, then join one row per order. The rule: aggregate at the grain where the measure lives.

exercises.q: Design the accuracy evaluation for a text-to-SQL system before launch. What do you compare, and what are the traps?
exercises.a: Build a golden set of 150+ real questions with a reference SQL written by an analyst. Score by execution accuracy: run both queries and compare result sets, not SQL text, because many different queries are correct. Traps: (1) row order, so compare as multisets unless the question asks for an order; (2) floats, so compare with a tolerance; (3) extra columns, so decide whether to compare only the requested columns; (4) a query that matches on today's data by accident, so run against a second database snapshot or perturbed data; (5) ambiguous questions, so either rewrite them or accept several references. Slice results by difficulty (single table, joins, nested, date logic). Public benchmarks such as Spider and BIRD use execution-based scoring for the same reasons.

interview.q: What is text-to-SQL and what is its biggest risk?
interview.a: Text-to-SQL takes a natural-language question, generates SQL against a known schema, runs it and returns the answer in words. It removes the bottleneck of waiting for someone who knows SQL and the schema. The biggest risk is not an error, which is visible, but a query that runs and returns a plausible wrong number, for example through a join that double counts or a filter that misses rows. Those get trusted and acted on, so validation, transparency (showing the SQL) and evaluation matter as much as generation.

interview.q: How do you measure text-to-SQL accuracy?
interview.a: Execution accuracy on a golden set: for each question, run the generated SQL and a reference SQL and compare the result sets, allowing for row order and float tolerance. Comparing SQL text (exact match) is too strict, because many queries are equivalent. I also track how often the query errors, how often it needed a retry, and latency. And I slice by question type, since joins and date logic usually fail more than single-table lookups. Spider and BIRD are the public benchmarks to know, but my own schema's golden set is what decides.

interview.q: Leadership wants a "chat with the warehouse" tool across 400 tables next quarter. How do you scope it to succeed?
interview.a: Narrow it first. Pick one domain, say sales, with 10 to 20 curated views in a semantic layer: clear names, documented metric definitions, joins baked in. Build a golden set of 150 real questions from that team's queue and measure execution accuracy before launch. Ship with guardrails: read-only role, timeouts, cost caps, SQL shown with each answer, clarifying questions for ambiguous asks, and analyst review for anything feeding finance. Expand domain by domain, each with its own views and golden set. The model is the easy part; the semantic layer and evaluation are the project.

analogy: Asking someone to find a book in a library they have never visited is hopeless; giving them the floor map, the section labels and two example call numbers makes it easy. The schema is the map, column descriptions are the labels, and few-shot examples are the sample call numbers. For a huge library you give them only the map of the right floor. The analogy breaks because a visitor who reaches the wrong shelf notices; a model given the wrong tables will still write a query, just against the wrong data.

scale.title: 400 tables: dump the schema or retrieve it?
scale.html:
Assumptions: a warehouse with 400 tables, 25 columns each on average, about 12 tokens per column line including a short comment and 20 tokens per table header (estimate; count with your tokenizer), 5,000 questions a day, a model at $2 per million input tokens (Anthropic models overview, checked 2026-11-03).

  1. Full schema size. 400 x (20 + 25 x 12) = 400 x 320 = 128,000 tokens. It fits in a 1 M-token window, so the limit is not the window. It is cost and focus.
  2. Full schema cost. 128,000 x $2 / 1 M = $0.256 per question, $1,280 a day, and the model has 394 tables it should ignore, several with similar names.
  3. Retrieved schema. Embed one card per table (name, description, column names, grain, join keys). Retrieve the top 6: 6 x 320 = 1,920 tokens, plus about 1,000 for sample rows and value notes, 600 for two few-shot examples and 200 for instructions = about 3,700 tokens. 3,700 x $2 / 1 M = $0.0074, about $37 a day.
  4. The new failure. If retrieval misses a needed table (often a bridge table such as order_items), the SQL either fails or quietly answers a different question. So measure table recall@6 on a golden set of questions labelled with the tables their reference SQL uses.
  5. Close the gap. After retrieval, add foreign-key neighbours of the retrieved tables (one hop). If that brings the prompt to 10 tables, it is still only about 5,000 tokens.

Result: about 35 times cheaper and usually more accurate, provided table recall is measured, not assumed.

lab.look_for: Find where the lab builds the schema context for the prompt (schema grounding). Run the question set once as-is, then remove the column descriptions or sample values from the context and run again: execution accuracy should drop, typically on questions that depend on value formats or which column holds what. Put them back and add one few-shot example matching a failing question's pattern to see it recover.

quiz.q: A user asks for "revenue from Germany". The model writes WHERE country = 'DE' but the column stores 'Germany'. The query returns 0 rows. What prevents this most directly?

options.t: Sample rows or a value note in the schema context showing that country holds full names like 'Germany'.
options.why: The model could not know the value format from the column name alone. One sample row or a short comment fixes it, and it is cheap.

options.t: A larger model.
options.why: No model can know your data's value conventions without being shown them. Bigger models guess better on average, but they still guess.

options.t: A self-correction loop.
options.why: The query does not error; it returns 0 rows. An error-driven loop never fires unless you also treat empty results as a signal.

options.t: Lower temperature.
options.why: Deterministic sampling makes the same wrong guess every time. The missing piece is information, not randomness.

exercises.q: A mart has 60 tables averaging 18 columns. Using 12 tokens per column and 20 per table header, estimate the full schema in tokens and the cost per question at $2 per million input tokens.
exercises.a: Per table: 20 + 18 x 12 = 236 tokens. 60 x 236 = 14,160 tokens. Cost = 14,160 x $2 / 1 M = $0.028 per question. At this size dumping the whole schema can be reasonable; retrieval pays off as tables grow or when similar tables confuse the model.

exercises.q: Write the schema-context lines for a hostile table: f_txn_d(cid INT, amt_c BIGINT, st SMALLINT, dt INT), where amt_c is amount in cents, st 1 = paid and 2 = refunded, dt is a date as YYYYMMDD.
exercises.a:
Table f_txn_d(cid INT, amt_c BIGINT, st SMALLINT, dt INT)
  -- one row per transaction. cid joins customers.id.
  -- amt_c is the amount in CENTS: divide by 100.0 for currency.
  -- st: 1 = paid, 2 = refunded. Revenue uses st = 1 only.
  -- dt is an integer date YYYYMMDD, e.g. 20250603. Filter 2025 with dt BETWEEN 20250101 AND 20251231.
Sample: (42, 12000, 1, 20250603)
Better long-term: a view transactions(customer_id, amount_usd, status, txn_date DATE) so the model never sees the raw encoding.

exercises.q: Design schema retrieval for 400 tables and the eval that proves it works.
exercises.a: Index one card per table: name, a human-written description, column names with short meanings, grain, primary and foreign keys, and two or three questions it answers. Optionally index metric definitions and example Q-to-SQL pairs as separate searchable items. At query time, use hybrid retrieval (BM25 catches exact column or table names, dense catches meaning), take the top 6, then add one-hop foreign-key neighbours. Eval: a golden set of 150+ questions, each with the set of tables in its reference SQL. Report table recall@k (all needed tables retrieved), prompt size, and end-to-end execution accuracy. If execution accuracy fails while table recall is high, the problem is the prompt or examples, not retrieval.

interview.q: What do you put in a text-to-SQL prompt?
interview.a: The SQL dialect, an instruction to use only the listed tables and columns and to return a single SELECT, the schema for the relevant tables with column types and join keys, short descriptions of non-obvious columns, a sample row or value notes so the model sees formats like 'Canada' versus 'CA', and two or three example question-and-SQL pairs showing house conventions such as filtering paid orders. Then the question. Each part removes a specific guessing failure.

interview.q: How do you handle a schema too big for the prompt?
interview.a: Schema retrieval, which is RAG over metadata. I index each table with a description, columns, grain and keys, retrieve the few most relevant tables for each question, and add their foreign-key neighbours so join bridges are not lost. I measure table recall on a golden set because a missed table silently breaks the query. Hybrid search helps, since users often mention exact column or table names. Where possible I also point retrieval at curated views rather than raw tables, which shrinks the search space and removes ambiguity.

interview.q: Accuracy plateaued at 78% despite better prompts. Where would you invest next?
interview.a: In the data surface, not the prompt. I read the failures and usually find ambiguous metrics, cryptic columns, encoded statuses and multi-hop joins. So I build a semantic layer: views with readable names and joins baked in, documented metric definitions, and a library of verified example queries retrieved as few-shot examples per question. I add clarifying questions for ambiguous asks rather than guessing. Then re-run the golden set by slice. Prompt tweaks give a few points; a good semantic layer often moves accuracy far more, because it turns the problem into one the model rarely gets wrong.

analogy: Letting a model write SQL is like letting a new driver take the family car. You tell them to drive carefully (the prompt), but you also give them a car with a speed limiter (timeout), a small fuel tank (row and cost caps), and no keys to the truck (a read-only account). If they ignore your advice, the car itself still will not do the dangerous thing. The analogy breaks because a new driver is not being actively tricked; a model can be prompt-injected by text hidden in the very data it reads.

scale.title: Guarding a 2 TB fact table on Postgres, BigQuery and Snowflake
scale.html:
Assumptions: a 2 TB orders fact table, a scan rate of about 1 GB/s on the read replica (measure yours), rows of about 200 bytes, and a model that occasionally forgets a WHERE clause.

  1. The runaway. A full scan of 2 TB at 1 GB/s is 2,000 s, about 33 minutes of replica time per bad query. Ten users retrying makes the replica useless for everyone.
  2. Postgres: timeout. statement_timeout aborts any statement that runs longer than the value; the default 0 disables it (Postgres docs). Set it on the text-to-SQL role, e.g. 15 s, so the 33-minute scan dies after 15 seconds.
  3. Postgres: permissions. GRANT only SELECT on the analytics schema to that role. default_transaction_read_only = on adds a second layer, but a session can change it, so the GRANT is the real wall.
  4. Row cap. 1,000 rows x 200 bytes = 200 KB to the app. An uncapped SELECT * of 10 M rows is 2 GB pulled into your API process.
  5. BigQuery is different. Google's docs say a LIMIT clause does not reduce compute cost on non-clustered tables; use the maximum bytes billed setting, which fails the query before it runs if the estimate is over the limit, without a charge (BigQuery cost best practices). A row LIMIT protects your app, not your bill.
  6. Snowflake. STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS defaults to two days (Snowflake parameters). Set it low on the warehouse or user that serves the tool.

Same idea in every engine: the limits live in the database, configured for the model's account, not in the prompt.

lab.look_for: Find the lab's SELECT-only validation and row limit. Feed it a few hostile strings by hand: a DELETE, a SELECT followed by a semicolon and DROP TABLE, and a CTE that ends in a DELETE (WITH x AS (SELECT 1) DELETE FROM t), which starts with WITH and so passes a naive prefix check. Note which layer stops each one. Then ask a question whose correct answer has its own LIMIT 3 and confirm the row-limit wrapper does not break it.

quiz.q: Your text-to-SQL tool on BigQuery appends LIMIT 1000 to every query. A user's question triggers a SELECT over a 5 TB non-clustered table. What does the LIMIT do for cost?

options.t: Nothing for compute cost; the table is still scanned. Use maximum bytes billed to fail the query before it runs.
options.why: Google's cost docs state that LIMIT does not reduce compute cost on non-clustered tables. Maximum bytes billed checks the estimated bytes up front and fails the query without a charge.

options.t: It cuts the scan to 1,000 rows' worth of bytes.
options.why: BigQuery's on-demand cost depends on bytes read, and LIMIT does not reduce bytes read on non-clustered tables.

options.t: It makes the query read-only.
options.why: LIMIT has nothing to do with permissions. Read-only access comes from the IAM roles of the account running the query.

options.t: It blocks the query because 5 TB is above the limit.
options.why: LIMIT counts output rows, not bytes scanned. It never blocks a query for scanning too much.

exercises.q: In SQLite, WITH x AS (SELECT 1) DELETE FROM orders starts with WITH. Does the page's validate() let it through, and what stops it?
exercises.a: validate() lets it through: there is no semicolon and it starts with "with". SQLite does allow a WITH clause in front of INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE (SQLite WITH docs). What stops it: the read-only connection (mode=ro) would reject the write, and the row-limit wrapper SELECT * FROM (...) is a syntax error for a DELETE. This is why the page has several layers; the prefix check alone is not enough.

exercises.q: Write the Postgres setup for a text-to-SQL role that can only read the analytics schema, times out after 15 s and defaults to read-only transactions.
exercises.a:
CREATE ROLE nl2sql LOGIN PASSWORD '...';  -- store it in a secret manager
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA analytics TO nl2sql;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA analytics TO nl2sql;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA analytics GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO nl2sql;
ALTER ROLE nl2sql SET statement_timeout = '15s';
ALTER ROLE nl2sql SET default_transaction_read_only = on;
The GRANTs are the hard guarantee; the role settings are defaults that the session could override, so they are a second layer. Point the role at a read replica so even an allowed heavy query cannot slow production writes.

exercises.q: A support agent uses the tool and asks "show me all employees and their salaries". The role can read the HR schema. Nothing technical stops it. Redesign access so the tool respects who is asking.
exercises.a: Make the database enforce the user's permissions, not the tool's. Options: run each query under the end user's identity (or a role mapped to their group) so existing grants apply; expose only curated views that exclude sensitive columns, with column-level grants; add row-level security policies for per-team data. Keep the tool's own account at the minimum: views only, no raw HR tables. Then add a policy check before execution that blocks queries touching tagged sensitive columns for non-authorized users, and log every query with the requesting user. The model should never be the component deciding who may see salaries.

interview.q: Why is "only write SELECT statements" in the prompt not enough?
interview.a: Because a prompt is a request, not a control. The model usually follows it, but a prompt injection, hidden in a question or in data the model reads, can override it, and models also make plain mistakes. If the code runs whatever comes back on a read-write connection, one bad output can delete data. The real protection is a read-only database account, plus validation, a timeout and a row cap in code. The prompt instruction stays, as a way to reduce bad generations, not as the safety mechanism.

interview.q: List the layers you would put around generated SQL, strongest first.
interview.a: One: a least-privilege database account, SELECT only, ideally on curated views and a read replica, which makes writes impossible. Two: a statement timeout and, on BigQuery, maximum bytes billed, which bound cost and load in the engine. Three: code validation, using a SQL parser to allow only a single SELECT rather than string matching. Four: a row cap by wrapping the query. Five: parameterizing any user-supplied literals. Six: logging every query with the user. Each layer assumes the others can fail.

interview.q: How do prompt injection risks differ for text-to-SQL compared with a RAG chatbot?
interview.a: In RAG, injected text mostly corrupts the answer or tries to exfiltrate data through the output. In text-to-SQL the model's output is executed, so injection can become an action: a write, a huge scan, or a query reading data the user should not see. Sources of injection include the question, column comments and data values pulled into few-shot examples or result summaries. The defence is to treat generated SQL as untrusted code: least-privilege execution under the user's own permissions, engine-level limits, parser-based allowlists, and never feeding raw result data back to the model without care. OWASP lists prompt injection as the top LLM risk for this reason.

analogy: It is like a spelling test where the teacher circles the exact wrong letter and lets you try again twice. With the circle you fix it almost every time; if the teacher just said "wrong, try again", you would probably make the same mistake. The analogy breaks because the database only circles mistakes that break the rules of SQL; a query that is valid but answers the wrong question gets no circle at all.

scale.title: What a 3-try loop buys on 1,000 questions, and what it cannot fix
scale.html:
Assumptions (measure your own): 82% of first-try queries run without error, each retry fixes 70% of the remaining errors, max_tries = 3 (one try plus two retries), 4,000 input and 200 output tokens per call, about 4,400 input on retries because they carry the error and the failed SQL, prices of $2 / $10 per million input / output tokens (Anthropic models overview, checked 2026-11-03).

  1. After try 1: 820 of 1,000 run; 180 error.
  2. After try 2: 180 x 0.7 = 126 fixed, 946 run (94.6%); 54 still failing.
  3. After try 3: 54 x 0.7 = 37.8 fixed, about 984 run (98.4%); about 16 give up gracefully with a message.
  4. Calls per question. 1 + 0.18 + 0.054 = 1.234 on average.
  5. Cost. First call = 4,000 x $2 / 1 M + 200 x $10 / 1 M = $0.010. Retry = 4,400 x $2 / 1 M + $0.002 = $0.0108. Average = $0.010 + 0.234 x $0.0108 = about $0.0125 a question, $12.50 per 1,000.
  6. The ceiling. Suppose execution accuracy against reference answers is 86%. Then 984 - 860 = 124 queries ran fine and returned the wrong result. The error loop cannot touch those: there was no error. They need result-shape checks, clarifying questions and the semantic layer.

So the loop takes "runs" from 82% to 98%, cheaply. "Correct" is a separate number that you must measure separately.

lab.look_for: The lab's self-correction loop feeds the SQL error back to the model and retries. Count, from its output, how many questions succeeded on the first try, how many needed a retry, and how many gave up. Then compare "ran without error" with the execution-accuracy score: the gap between them is the wrong-but-runs share that error feedback cannot fix. Try setting the retry cap to 1 to see the first-try rate on its own.

quiz.q: Your loop sees the same error three times in a row: the model keeps producing identical SQL. What is the best change?

options.t: Detect a repeated query or error and stop early, or change the feedback (add the real column list for the table named in the error) before retrying.
options.why: Retrying with the same input usually gets the same output. Either give the model new information, such as the actual columns, or stop and fail gracefully instead of paying for identical failures.

options.t: Raise max_tries to 10.
options.why: If the model is stuck, more identical retries just cost more and delay the user.

options.t: Raise the temperature on retries.
options.why: More randomness may change the SQL but not toward correctness, and many hosted models no longer accept temperature changes. New information is what helps.

options.t: Remove the schema from retries to save tokens.
options.why: The schema is exactly what the model needs to fix a wrong column. Removing it makes the fix less likely.

exercises.q: First-try success is 75% and each retry fixes 60% of remaining errors. With max_tries = 3, what fraction of queries end up running, and how many calls per question on average?
exercises.a: After try 1: 75% run, 25% fail. Try 2 fixes 25% x 0.6 = 15%, total 90%, 10% fail. Try 3 fixes 10% x 0.6 = 6%, total 96%, 4% give up. Average calls = 1 + 0.25 + 0.10 = 1.35.

exercises.q: Write three result-shape checks that would catch wrong-but-runs answers, and the feedback you would send to the model for each.
exercises.a: (1) The question asks for one number ("how many", "total") but the result has many rows: "The question expects a single value but the query returned 4,210 rows. Aggregate it." (2) A count or sum is far larger than the table's row count or known totals, a sign of fan-out: "The sum is larger than the total of all orders; check for a join that duplicates rows." (3) An empty result for a question that names a value: "No rows matched country = 'DE'. Sample values for country are 'Germany', 'Canada'." Each turns a silent wrong answer into an observation the loop can act on, still bounded by max_tries.

exercises.q: Design an experiment to show leadership what the self-correction loop is worth, honestly.
exercises.a: Use the golden set (150+ questions with reference SQL). Run three configurations on the same questions and the same model: (A) single shot, (B) error feedback with max_tries = 3, (C) B plus result-shape checks and clarifying questions for flagged ambiguous ones. Report for each: ran-without-error rate, execution accuracy, average calls, p95 latency and cost per 1,000 questions. Use a paired comparison on the same questions (count questions fixed and broken between configs) to see whether gains beat noise. Expect B to raise the run rate a lot and execution accuracy less; C to close part of the remaining gap. Presenting both numbers stops anyone confusing "it runs" with "it is right".

interview.q: How does a self-correcting SQL agent work?
interview.a: It runs the generated SQL with a safe read-only runner. If the database returns an error, the agent sends the exact error message and the failed query back to the model and asks for a fix, then tries again, up to a small limit such as three tries. On success it returns the rows and the SQL for transparency; on repeated failure it stops and tells the user. It works because databases give precise errors like "no such column", which tell the model exactly what to change.

interview.q: Why cap retries, and what else should stop the loop early?
interview.a: Some questions cannot be answered from the schema at all, and a stuck model will produce the same failure again, so an uncapped loop burns time and money with no gain. Two or three tries catch most fixable errors. Stop earlier when the same SQL or the same error repeats, when a per-request token or time budget runs out, or when the error is not fixable by rewriting, such as a permission denied or timeout, which should go to the user or an operator rather than back to the model.

interview.q: Error-driven self-correction raised your run rate to 98% but users still find wrong numbers. What do you do next?
interview.a: Recognize the loop only fixes queries that fail, so I measure execution accuracy separately and read the runs-but-wrong cases. Typical causes: fan-out joins, wrong filters, wrong metric definitions, and ambiguous questions. Fixes in order of leverage: a semantic layer with canonical metric views; result-shape and sanity checks fed back into the same bounded loop; clarifying questions when the question maps to several plausible queries; showing SQL and row counts in the UI; and a growing golden set from user-reported errors, gated in CI. The Self-Debugging and DIN-SQL papers show the feedback idea; the semantic layer is what makes answers right.
